en: The *Jaṭāmaṇi-vyākhyāna*: Om. When it is stated, "One who has the qualification for the study of the *jaṭā*," the qualified person is described by the statement, "one who knows the *Prātiśākhya* and other sciences. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), it is meant that he is one who has mastered the nine *Śikṣās*, as well as the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and so forth; he must possess subtle intellect and capability. He must be capable of correct pronunciation, free from nervousness in an assembly—such a person is fit to recite the *jaṭā*. (1)

Now, since only the *saṃhitā* is useful for the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, one might argue that the *pada-pāṭha* should also be studied; for, in the absence of study according to the divisions of words (*pada*), there would be no knowledge of word-boundaries within the *saṃhitā*, and because the rule "Now, at the beginning and end, there is division" exists in the *Prātiśākhya* as a characteristic applying to each word.

Since it is understood that the fruit [of study] is realized through gradual study—based on the principle that "one who is perfected in study in due order attains the state of a deity"—and since there exists a sequential characteristic for study, it must be studied in sequence. Thus, in response to the doubt as to how there can be a study of the *jaṭā* (the matted-text) given the absence of authority for such a study, the very authority for the *jaṭā* is stated by the words beginning with "tasyāṃ pramāṇam" (the authority for that).

Regarding the measure for that *jaṭā* (interwoven recitation), it should be understood from the rule in the first chapter of the *Prātiśākhya*, under the section on *visarjanīya* concerning the substitution of *repha*, that this applies even to a following [word] due to the word "api" (*even*) in the sūtra, and also by virtue of the archaic term "na dhāma. This is the syntactical connection. The word "api" (*even*) in the sūtra indicates that it refers to what follows in the *āvṛt* (recitation). That *visarjanīya* which follows in the *āvṛt* becomes *repha* if it is followed [by a vowel]. There is no example of this in *saṃhitā*; the example is found only in the *jaṭā*. For instance: [Example omitted in source text]

Thus, [the term] *śruta* is understood as "heard" (*śruta-riti*). Why [is the condition] "followed by *āvṛt*" (*āvṛtpara*) stated? [It is so that] in the case of *prahārāvayor vaiśritaḥ*, because there is no subsequent *āvṛt*, [the rule] should not apply; therefore, this sūtra is a definition of *jaṭā*. Furthermore, regarding the junction (*saṃdhi*) in the study of *jaṭā*, since the word *na dhāma* is an archaic (*ārṣa*) form, the mention of "archaic" (*ārṣa*) implies the exclusion of human (secular) forms.

And thus, there is no conventional usage regarding the *padas*, *kramas*, *jaṭās*, and so forth as being anything other than the *saṃhitā* or as being of human origin. Furthermore, in the *Havārabhāra* and other sūtras, the mention of *abibhar* is illustrated only in the case of the *jaṭā*; likewise, the mention of *pada* is also illustrated only in the case of the *jaṭā*. For example: *abibhastantamabibharabibhastam* (where the *jaṭā* is: *abibhar abibhar abibhar*), and *marutāṃ pitaḥ pitarmmarutāmmarutāṃ pitaḥ* (where the *jaṭā* is: *marutām pitaḥ marutām pitaḥ*). Thus, in the study of the *jaṭā*, there is a junction of authoritative sources (*pramāṇasaṃdhi*).

Now, a doubt has been raised as to what kind of *jaṭā* (interwoven recitation) is the authority for the study of the *Jaṭā*: in response to this, he states that "the junction (*sandhi*) of the *jaṭā* is fivefold," meaning there are five types of junctions. They are: *bhakṣā*, *ā*, *ābhakṣa*, *bhakṣabhakṣa*, and *bhakṣā*. The junction between the beginning and the end is designated as *ārṣa* (Vedic/authoritative), while the other junctions are *anārṣa* (non-Vedic). Now, when it was asked what kind of *jaṭā* is, it was stated that the *jaṭā* consists of exactly five junctions; however, since eight junctions exist in the cases of *trikrama* (three-word combinations), how is this [fivefold division] possible? In response to this doubt, he says: "In the *trikramas*... [and so forth].

In the *trikramas*, the two [consonants] at the beginning and the two at the end are designated as *ārṣa* (archaic); the other *sandhis* are *anārṣaka* (non-archaic). For example: *udgātā*, *ārohati*, *rohati rohati*, *rohatyā*, *odgātā*, *udgātodgātā*, *udgātā*, *ārohati*, *ṛcā*, *āsādayati*, *sādayati sādayati*, *sādayityā*, *ārccā*, *ṛcarccā*, *ṛcā*, *āsādayati*. Regarding the doubt as to what the *jaṭā* and *kīdṛk* [forms] are like, he states another rule as well.

"Regarding the two words": having recited the two words in direct order (*anukrama*), which is the traditional method of the seers (*ārṣa*), one should then recite them again in reverse order (*vyutkrama*), in inverted order (*viloma*), in upward order (*utkrama*), and in forward order (*anuloma*). Having first recited the two words in direct order, then again in reverse order, and yet again in reverse order, one should employ them together with their accents (*svara*) without transgressing the rules for accents prescribed in the *Prātiśākhya*. For example:
*vadantyakūṭayākūṭayā vadanti vadantyakūṭayā* (6). "According to the rule" (*nyāyāt*).

The meaning is that when there is a reversal of what is perceived according to logic (*nyāya*), authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and by way of illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), such a *sandhi* is designated as "tangled" (*jaṭā*).

(7) Regarding the phrase "wherein [it is] archaic" (*yatrārṣe*): in the archaic [Vedic] usage, a manifested *sandhi* is not intended; rather, if an unmanifested *sandhi* should appear in the "tangled" state, that is stated as an illustration in the *Aruṇa-brāhmaṇa*. For example: *nṛṣadevaḍvaṇṇṛṣade nṛṣadevaṭ*. (8)
He explains the method of pronouncing the *jaṭā*:

"The word *sakṛt* and so forth. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) means *sakṛt*; the second [instance] is a double repetition; then again the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) means *sakṛt*. Immediately thereafter, the *jaṭā* is proclaimed by the wise as being joined according to the sequence. For example: *upopedidupopopopet* (9).
He explains the method of the *jaṭā* in the context of the triple-sequence (*trikrama*).

Regarding the phrase "of the *trikrama*": in the context of the *trikrama*, having first stated the initial word (*ādipada*), the final word (*antapada*) is stated next; after that, the middle word (*madhyamapada*); after that, the initial word again; then the initial word once more; after that, the middle word; and finally, the final word is stated. This is to be understood as the *trikrama-jaṭā*. For example: *bhūtvā harada harat bhūtvā bhūtvā harat* (10).
In the context of the *trikrama*, there are two words repeated six times; likewise, one should state nine words (13).

If there is no difference between the vowels and consonants in two words, then the *jaṭā* [interlacing] is prescribed by the learned only for sequential pronunciation (*kramoccāraṇa*). For example: *adantyadanti*, *namo namaḥ*. Why "difference in vowels" (*svarabheda*)? Consider: *tarati tarati tarati tarati tarati tarati*. Why "difference in consonants" (*varṇabheda*)? Consider: *asūrttāsūrttāsūrttāsūrttāsūrttāsūrttā*. [The rule continues:
"Omission (*lopa*), non-omission (*alopa*), and the substitution of *ṣatva*."

The meaning is that elision (*lopa*), non-elision (*alopa*), the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*), the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*), the substitution of *v* (*vatvādeśa*), and augmentations (*āgama*)—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including [changes] such as the *visarjanīya*—occur in the *jaṭā* exactly as they occur according to their application in the *saṃhitā*. For example: *somapratipratiṣomasomaprati*; *enamindra indra eṇamenamindraḥ*; *anuṣṭubhāpari paryanuṣṭubhānuṣṭubhāpari*; *aśva ṛṣabha ṛṣabho aśvo'śva ṛṣabhaḥ*; *aṃgirobhyassvāhā svāhāṃgirobhyo aṃgirobhyassvāhā*.

Let it be for those that follow; let it be for those that follow. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), as follows: *syapraprasyasyapra*. For [in the case of] *na hyatyanuṣṭubanuṣṭumnahyati nahyatyanuṣṭup* (15), in the phrase *anvatapyanta*, since the vowels *i* and *u* were previously changed to *y* and *v* respectively by the rule of *yaṇ*-substitution, there would be no instance for the application of the *agni* rule thereafter; therefore, the mention of *agni* is for the purpose of establishing a restriction (*niyama*) to prevent the application of elision (*lopa*). As follows: *agnayo'nvatapyantānvatapyantāgnayo'gnayo'nvatapyanta* (16).

Regarding the apprehension [of a word], those who hold the view of *jaṭā* have stated that when one word is intended, it is apprehended as being directed toward that single word, such that it should not be apprehended elsewhere. This statement applies only to the scope of the mere fact that "they regret" (anvatapyante). 17.

In the phrase *tathaivāśvājanī*, the meaning of *tathaiva* (in that very same way) is that they regret it here just as [they did] there. When the vowel *ā* is heard and a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, then, in the reverse order at the time of the *jaṭā* arrangement, there is indeed elision (*lopa*). For example: *aśvājani pracetasaḥ*, *pracetasaḥ aśvājanyāḥ*, *aśvājani pracetasaḥ*. Regarding this, the authors of the *Śikṣā* say: "As for what is called the hearing of the sound *aśva*, which they know occurs in both the whole word and the divided part—it is to be understood through the compound itself; having seen *aśvājani*, it is so described."

Thus, in a single word (*samānapada*), there is only elision (*alopa*). "Aśvājanipracetasaḥ" [is explained as] "of the wise ones (*pracetasaḥ*) born from the noble lineage of horses (*aśvājanya-*)". This is an alternative reading. 18.
Likewise, [the form] "iyātām".

In the case of *aśvājanī*, the meaning is "just as [before]. In the example *eyātāṃ brāhmaṇāya*, by the rule *tatra pūrvam* (Pāṇini 6.1.84), when the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is formed according to the rule *dīrghaṃ smānākṣare savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the vowel *e*—which follows an *i*-vowel—is subsequently subject to the rule *ekāramāpnoti* (becomes *e*). For example: *eyātāṃ brāhmaṇāya brāhmaṇāyaiyātāmeyātāṃ brāhmaṇāya*. Furthermore, in *etya punaḥ punaretya*, the authors of the *Śikṣā* state: "In *eyātāṃ brāhmaṇāya*, however, the vowel *e* should remain uncombined (*asandhita*)."

If the subsequent vowel (*paravarṇa*) is joined [with the preceding], the Lord of the Gaṇas (Śiva) prohibits it; thus, in the case of *eyātām brāhmaṇāya*, there is only the vowel *e*. Since this statement is not widely accepted, this rule is simply not admitted. When the substitution of *cha* (for *śa*) would otherwise apply:

In the case of *śnathadvṛtram*, when the *jaṭā* (interwoven) sandhi occurs, the letter *takāra* would undergo *chatva* (substitution with *ch*) according to the rule *śacachaparaḥ*. However, since the rule *sparśapūrvaḥ śakāraśchakāram* applies, there is an occasion for *chatva*. At the time of forming the *jaṭā*, because the preceding sound is not *śa*, it does not become *ākāra*; rather, the meaning is that the original *nakāra* remains. Thus: *śnathadvṛttram*, *vṛttraḥ śnathat*, *śnathadvṛttram*. (20)

Regarding the word *anu*: when the vowel *u* of the word *anu*—specifically the *u* and *i* vowels of the word *anu*—is changed to *v*, then in the place where the *u* is modified to *v*, there is no elision (*lopa*) in the *jaṭā* (interwoven) arrangement; rather, it is determined that the *a* [of the preceding word] is elided. Thus: *anugāvaḥ gāvaḥ anu* becomes *anugāvaḥ*. Regarding the word *anu*: when the vowel *u* of the word *anu* is changed to *v* as previously described, just as there is elision in *saṃhitā*, so too should there be elision here. Thus: *gāvaḥ anu* becomes *gāvo'nugāvaḥ*; *gāvaḥ anu* becomes *gāvo'nu*.

Regarding those [words] that possess short vowels: for all words possessing short vowels, shortness is to be understood in the *pūrvapauruṣa* (the first half). By the term "possessing short vowels," one refers to cases such as "atha" at the beginning and "uttare vibhāge" (in the subsequent division) and so forth. At the time of the *jaṭā* arrangement, there is lengthening at the beginning and the end of the *uttarapauruṣa* (the second half); thus, the meaning is that there is a short vowel in the middle. As an example in the *pūrvapauruṣa*: *hiṣṭhasthahihiṣṭha*. As an example in the *uttarapauruṣa*: *sthāmayobhuvo mayo bhuvasthasthāmayo bhuvaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase *sthām-ayo-bhuvaḥ*, the author of the *Tribhāṣyaratna* has stated that in the case of *jaṭā*, when the word *stha-* is pronounced a second time, a long vowel would otherwise result; however, since there is no separation from the subsequent word (*uttarapada*), this [long vowel] must not occur. 23.

That which possesses the status of a *pragraha* in an *ārṣa* [word] also possesses the status of a *pragraha* when it occurs in a non-*ārṣa* [word]. This means that according to the definition stated in the *Prātiśākhya*, beginning with the section "Now, the *pragrahas*," in that manner there shall be no distinction in the case of human (non-Vedic) usage. For example: *antarbhariṣyantī*, *bhariṣyantī*, *antarantarbhariṣyantī*. What is the purpose of the rule "it has the status of a *pragraha* in an *ārṣa* [word]"? [Consider the example: *tāvabrūtāṃ sarve* and *āstāntetaḥ*. In these cases, the application of the *ārṣa* restriction would result in the status of *pragraha*; this is not desired. 24.

"Or the principal [word] is the cause (nimitta)": this means that the principal word is the part of the compound that undergoes the grammatical operation. Alternatively, "the cause" refers to the specific position where the two-word form is prescribed; if there is a transposition in that position at the time of forming the *jaṭā* (interwoven) arrangement, then the entire two-word form is to be taken. In the regular sequence (*krama*), however, it is taken from one part [only]. For example: *no'gnayo agnayo no'gnayaḥ*. 25.

Regarding the cause of the two words: wherever there is a cause for the two words, in that case, when one [word] is absent during the time of *jaṭā*, the vowel is stated to be as in *saṃhitā*. For example, *indraṇo na* becomes *indrendraṇaḥ*. Here, it occurs even in the absence of the prefix *sam*. 26.

[This applies] to *ca* and the others alone; that is to say, [it applies] to indeclinables (*avyaya*). When an indeclinable follows, there is the elision (*lopa*) of *va*; that is to say, the elision of the letter *v*. It is stated by the grammatical treatise itself: "When followed by *ak* or *kvip*, there is elision of the *m*; when preceded by *ut* and followed by a consonant, there is elision of the *s*; and in the case of *sthā* and *stambh*, there is elision of the *s*. Examples: *innunvidinnu*, *nvaivainunvai*, *tvaivaitutvai*. Why specify "when an indeclinable follows"? Consider: *viduṣo nunu viduṣo viduṣo nu* (O knower, come now, O knower, O knower, now), and *varuṇastu tuvaruṇo varuṇastu* (Varuṇa, indeed; quickly, Varuṇa; Varuṇa, indeed).

In the case of *vasatu* followed by *nuvasatu*, there is the elision of *vasatu nu*. As for the elision of the letter *m*: as in *pratyuṣṭaṃ rakṣaḥ* (the demon is burnt away) and *taṃ ṣaḍahāni* (those six days). As for the elision of the letter *s*: as in *sthānād udutthānāt* (from the place of rising), which becomes *sthānād ut*; and *sthāstan*. Regarding the rule "optionally after *bhoḥ*": what is the example? *svāyuṣod ut svāyuṣā* (O long-lived one, rise with your life-force), which becomes *svāyuṣot*; *syād ud ut syāt* (it may indeed arise), which becomes *syād ut*; *stomam ud ut stomaṃ* (the hymn, rise up, the hymn), which becomes *stomam ut*. 27.

The *makāra* which is in an *avagraha*: that *makāra* situated in an *avagraha*, when preceded by *saṃ*, is not elided for the sake of the *sāman*. As in *sammrājoravaḥ*. Why "in an *avagraha*"? [Because] in the case of *toterāyassandevī* within a *jaṭā*, this prohibition does not apply; thus, by the word "for" (*iti*), it indicates a different meaning. [Examples: *rāyassaṃ saṃrāyo rāyassaṃ*; *rājñe saṃ saṃ rājñe rājñe sam*; *rāṣṭreṇa saṃ saṃ rāṣṭreṇa rāṣṭreṇa sam*. The meaning is that a wise man should be recognized as such; otherwise, it would not be possible. 30.

Regarding the elision of *y*: when there is an elision of *y*, if it occurs preceded by the word *tiṣṭhanti*, then in the case of the inclusion [of the word] *ekayā*, the elision of *y* takes place. For example: *tiṣṭhantyekaikayā-ekaikayā-tiṣṭhanti tiṣṭhantyekaikayā*. At the time of forming *jaṭā*, even in the absence of the qualification by the word *tiṣṭhanti*, [the rule applies]; it does not depend on a specific cause. [Examples include: *ekaikayā stutayā*, *stutayaikaikayā*, *ekaikayā stutayā*. Thus, in the inclusion of the word *ekam* as qualified by the word *iti*, there is the elision of *m*.
In this case as well, one does not depend on a specific cause; for example, regarding matted hair (*jaṭā*): "Of each and every one of those, there is one for each. (31)

Regarding "from a conjoined [vowel]": as stated in the *Prātiśākhya*, "a single phoneme is called *apṛkta* when not conjoined," so too the technical term *apṛkta* means "not joined with a consonant. In both cases—conjoined (*pṛkta*) and unconjoined (*apṛkta*)—there is a long vowel in the conjunction. A *guṇa* vowel follows an *a*-vowel. For example: *upāt upāt upātu*; *uyantu yantu uyantu*; *ūṣuḥ uṣu*; *ūnu nūnu*; *ūtutūtu*. Following an *u*-vowel, for example: *utvā tvā avutvā*; *uhotā hotā vuhotā*.

By the two words *tat* and *tasmāt*, the preceding single-consonant (*apṛkta*) *u* becomes long even when followed [by another vowel] at the time of forming the *jaṭā* (interlocking) sandhi. Thus: *tadūtatadu*; *tasmādūtasmāttasmādu*. In instances other than these, when the augment *v* is applied, it is as follows: *sa uvusa*, *sa u*. 33.

In the case of *āyo'ddhvaryo krato*, the initial vowel *a* should be elided at the time of forming the *jaṭā* (interwoven) recitation, provided that it is an archaic (*ārṣa*) usage when [the preceding vowel] has been elided. For example: *janayatyaddhvaryo'ddhvaryo janayati*, *janayatyaddhvaryo*; *addhvaryo'veraveraddhvaryo'ddhvaryo'veḥ*; *agne dabdhāyodabdhāyognegnedabdhāyo*; *adabdhāyo'śītatano aśītatano adabdhāyo'dabdhāyo'śītatano*. Why specify "in the archaic usage" (*ārṣe*)? [To exclude cases where the rule does not apply.]

"O Adhvaryu, [the ladle] full of ghee; O Adhvaryu, the ladle full of ghee, O Adhvaryu; the ladle, O Adhvaryu, the ladle, O Adhvaryu; the ladle, O Adhvaryu. By the wise, this is not otherwise than what has been made by the Adhvaryu; the meaning is that there is a *pragraha* (prolongation) for anything other than this. For example: *avasātastabhāne tastabhāne avasāvasātasta bhāne*. 34.

The sequence should be understood as being like *saṃhitā*, and so too the *jaṭā*. Regarding what is stated in the *Prātiśākhya* in the rule "also the modified" (*vikṛtam*), that which is said applies at the time of the *jaṭā* as well: "the modified, the augment, and the elision" (*vikṛta-āgama-lopeṣu*) means "in cases of modification, augmentation, and elision. Thus, the meaning is that even at the time of the *jaṭā*, it is like *saṃhitā*. Examples: *nirṇenikte* from *nenikte* becomes *nirṇenikte*; *niśitāyān nirniśitāyān niśitāyān niḥ*. An example of an augment (*āgama*) is: *ṣaḍakṣareṇa* becomes *ṣaṭṭhaṣaṭṭhaṣaḍakṣareṇa* (ṣaṭ-ṭha-ṣaṭ-ṭha-ṣaḍakṣareṇa); *suparṇo'si* becomes *suparṇaḥ suparṇo'si* (suparṇaḥ-s-suparṇo'si). 36. [End of section on] the cause (*nimittī*).

But regarding the primary [element]: in the case of a prohibition, however, it is stated by another [authority] that due to the force of the cause (*nimitta*), there is a distinction in the *iṅg* (the marker); the meaning is that this concerns the scope of non-enumeration (*asaṃkhyāna*). It is not a positive injunction (*vidhi*), but rather it would be subject to prohibition.

||37|| Just as, moreover, by the force of the *kṛt* suffix, a positive injunction for the existence [of the suffix] is not desired in the case of *punar*—because of its predominance and because *kṛt* is the cause—this statement is undesirable. ||38||

[The change occurs] when followed by a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, because of the word "again" (*punar*). When a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix follows, the visarga of the word "again" (*punar*) undergoes the change to *s*. By the rule *nāddhvaraṃ ca*, the visarga of the word "again" situated within an *avagraha* is specifically prohibited. For example: *kṛdhi punaḥ*, *punaḥ kṛdhi*, *kṛdhipunaḥ*. Now, one might object: "Is there not already a prohibition for the word 'kṛdhi' itself by another rule? If you ask where that is, it is because a prohibition exists for [the word] when it contains the sound *dh*. To this, we reply: No. It is stated as follows:

In the presence of a *dhaṣ* sound, there is a prohibition [of *satva*] even when *kṣatra* follows *viśvataḥ*. This applies both when it is in a *pada* and when it is not in a *pada*, as seen in the *āvissūtra* regarding the word *kṛdhi*. The meaning of this is as follows: in the case of *viśvataḥ kṣatram*, the *visarjanīya* does not undergo *satva* (conversion to *s*) when followed by *kṣa* or *pa*, because of the prohibition in the presence of a *dhaṣ* sound. Even though the mention of *viśvataḥ* is explicitly stated (*kaṇṭhokta*), and although the prohibition in the presence of a *dhaṣ* sound is only half-stated (*ārddhika*), its explicit statement at the time of forming the *jaṭā* compound is not the determining factor. Furthermore, in the *āvissūtra*, the same prohibition in the presence of a *dhaṣ* sound applies even to the word *kṛdhi*.
It may be so. And thus, in the case of *kṛdhi punar*, there is no prohibition regarding [the substitution of] *dha* for *tha*.

(39) Regarding the rule for *satva* (the substitution of *s*), the condition of being preceded by *a* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) that applies even to long vowels (*dīrgha*). For example: *patiḥ pṛthivyāḥ*, *pṛthivyāḥ patiḥ*, *patiḥ pṛthivyāḥ*. Furthermore, it is seen in the case of *gnāspati*: "May Narāśaṃsa, the husband of the divine women (*gnās*), protect us. (40) In the rule *udathāparaśca*, the mention of the long vowel is also an indicator that includes the short vowel as well.

Likewise, regarding the rule *parivāprapara*, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the mention of the short vowel (*hrasva*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the long vowel (*dīrgha*) as well. For example: *vidvān athāthavidvān vidvān atha*; *prāñcau nirṇiṣprāñcau prāñcau niḥ*; *ātmanāparāniṣpra*; *bahiḥ prāṇo vai*. 43.

In which place: in the verse "sṛjyadhvam madhumatībhiḥ," the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur in the *pauruṣa* (human/ordinary) [text], because of the prohibition regarding that which contains the vowel *ṛ* or the letter *r*. Furthermore, this is because it is a general rule, as seen in "mahi tuvidirjapata. It should not be argued that *ṣ* would not occur here because the specific statement in the *pauruṣa* [text] takes precedence; for we see it in both "mahi" and "sapta": "sṛjyadhvaṃ mahi, mahi sṛjyadhvaṃ, sṛjyadhvaṃ mahi. (44)

And [the word *āyuḥ*] joined with the vowel *ṛ* and the letter *r*: when followed by the sound *niḥ*, or preceded by the word *āyuḥ*, the *visarjanīya* becomes *ṣ* when followed by the letter *t* at the time of *jaṭā*-formation. If it is argued that "there is no *ṣatva* (change to *ṣ*) because it is joined with the vowel *ṛ* and the letter *r*," [we reply]: no; for by the rule stating "it is based on ending in the letter *ṣ*," according to the opinion of Māhiṣeya himself, *ṣatva* indeed occurs. For example: *tṛtīyaṃ nirṇiṣṭṛtīyaṃ* [becomes] *tṛtīyanniḥ*; *triṣṭugāyurāyuṣṭriṣṭuk* [becomes] *triṣṭugāyuḥ*; *tasmādāyurāyuṣtasmāt* [becomes] *tasmādāyuḥ*. 45.

In the words *anvārabhya*, *annyaṃ*, and *annaṃ*, they do not state that the *ṇatva* (nasalization) occurs even when the *nakāra* is preceded by *parya*. [Examples are: *anvārabhya pari*, *paryanvārabhya*, *anvārabhya pari*; *annyaṃ pari*, *pari anyyam*, *annyaṃ pari*; *annaṃ pra*, *prānnam*, *mannam*, *annaṃ pra*. 49.
The *Śikṣā* and the *Prātiśākhya* contradict each other; if one says the *Śikṣā* is weaker, it is according to the maxim: "As a lion [is stronger] than a deer."

A wise person should first apply the change to *ṇ* (ṇatva) for the letter *n* that precedes *ṭ*; subsequently, the change to *ṇ* occurs for the letter *ṭ* by means of this rule: "when followed by a final [consonant], the best [nasal] of its own class [is substituted]. For example: *na + ānaḍ* becomes *ānaṇ* (as in *ānaṇo na ānaṭ*), and *nyamārṭ* becomes *mārṇṇi* (as in *nyamārḍamārṇṇi nyamārṭ*). Regarding the rules of the *Prātiśākhya*: whatever is not seen in these *Prātiśākhya* rules may occur through the force of other authorities (*sūtrāntara*). Thus, the meaning is that one should accept from among them that which is not stated in the *Prātiśākhya* but is not contradictory to it.
The letter *l*, when following a *ṭ*-class consonant (*ṭavarga*), undergoes the substitution of *ḍ*, being designated as *duśliṣṭa*. Thus, *labhate* becomes *viḍviḍḍabhate*; *labhate viṭ*. (55)

The word *pra*, *ā*, *upa*, and *apa*—preceded by these—undergoes the substitution of *āra*. For example: *ṛtunā prā prārtunartunā pra*; *ṛjumārjumṛjumā*; *ṛtenārttenarttenā*; *ṛtavyā upopārttavyāṛtavyā upa*; *ṛtūna*; *ṛtūnāmavāvārtūnāmṛtūnāmava*. The word *tu* (in the rule) serves the purpose of excluding the substitution of *āra* when preceded by other prefixes; as in *ṛddhyatepāparddhyata ṛddhyatepa*. 56.

The meaning is: for that very word-final *n* which, even when followed by a vowel, would undergo *yatva* (change to *y*) or *repha* (change to *r*) in an *ārṣa* (Vedic) context, that same word-final *n* shall undergo *repha* even when followed by another vowel in a non-*ārṣa* (secular) context. The purpose is that it should not be otherwise: [the rule] should apply in a secular context even when the Vedic cause (*nimitta*) is absent, and it should not apply in a Vedic context even when the secular cause is present. This is the intended sense.

Now, in the case of *athāsapatnān indrāgnī*, the *anusvāra* does not occur: *athāsapatnān sthapatnān athāthāsapatnān*; *āpo haviṣmān*, *haviṣmān āpaḥ*, *āpo haviṣmān*. (57) When there is no *y* or *r*, elsewhere—in cases such as the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (*ṣatva*) or *ṇ* for *n* (*ṇatva*)—the operation should be performed as in the direct order (*anuloma*). This is the meaning. (58) In the same way, in the word *mithunī* at the time of forming the *jaṭā* [interwoven] recitation, the substitution of *y* (*yatva*) is desired: *atha mithunī mithuny athātha mithunī*. And because it is seen [in the tradition], *mithunyaṣṭau* [is also valid]. (61)

The *tripadaprabhṛtinyāya* (the rule concerning three or more words) applies only to cases of elision (*lopa*) and non-elision (*alopa*). Regarding the word situated in an instance of elision and non-elision, some maintain that if it is joined with another [word], the property [of being a single word] does not exist; the previous property does not exist. (66) In the case of the vowels *e* and *o*, an *a*-vowel will be stated [as resulting from their combination]. At the time of forming the *jaṭā* (interwoven recitation), even if joined with a word other than those consisting of three or more [syllables], there is no "oneness with another" (*anyaikya*) here. (69)

Regarding the sequence of questions concerning the *jaṭā* (interwoven) formation starting from three words (*tripadaprabhṛti*): if, within that, one word undergoes the operation of elision (*lopa*) while another word does not, then whether the word subject to the operation of elision occurs before or after [the other], the rule for "starting from three words" (*tripadaprabhṛti*) applies there again. In the case of "starting from three words," by the inclusion of the term "etc. (*prabhṛti*), if five words are present, then both the "elided triad" (*lopatripadaprabhṛti*) and the "non-elided triad" (*alopatripadaprabhṛti*) apply; however, if the number of words is less than five, the principle of "starting from three words" (*tripadaprabhṛtinyāya*) does not exist.

In the sentences of the *Mantra* and *Brāhmaṇa*, however, there is a requirement for five words; yet, let it consist of two words, or three words, or even one word—in such cases, the rule beginning with "three words" (*tripada-prabhṛti-nyāya*) applies. Examples: in the phrase *saṃpaśyāmi*, the sentence *pari tvāgne* occurs in the first section of the *Agni-kāṇḍa*; [the repetitions] *tvāgne agne tvā tvāgne*; and in the section *bhūmir bhūmnā*, the sentence *punar ūrjā nivartasva* occurs in the section *viṣṇoḥ kramo 'si*.
[The repetitions] *agne iṣe 'gne agne iṣā*.

In the *anuvāka* beginning with "tvaṃ somatanūkṛtbhyaḥ," the sentence is "ayanno agniḥ"; in the *yājyā* [verse] beginning with "yastvāhṛdā," [the relevant portion is] "agniḥ varivo varivo agniragnirvarivaḥ. In the *anuvāka* beginning with "āpyāyatām," the sentence is "asya rātīyato hanta"; in the *anuvāka* beginning with "viṣṇoḥ kramo'si," [it is] "arātīyato hantā hantārātīyato'rātīyato hantā. In the *anuvāka* beginning with "bhūmirbhūmnā," the sentence is "saptate agne. It is just as in the case of "prācīm anv" and so forth.

"O Agni, [thou art] ours; O Agni, [thou art] ours; O Agni, [thou art] ours. In the section beginning with "Wide-ruling," there is the sentence beginning with "I have followed the waters. In the section beginning with "He who [thee] from the heart," [there is the phrase] "following the waters, following the waters, following the waters. In the section beginning with "I behold," there is the sentence beginning with "O Agni, [be] most near to us," as in the case of "Agni is the head. "Most near to us, most near to us, most near to us. In the section beginning with "We have gone to heaven," there is the sentence beginning with "Rich in cattle, O Agni," as in the case of "By Agni [we cross] over. "Rich in cattle, O Agni; O Agni, rich in cattle; rich in cattle, O Agni."

In the mantra *ye devā yajñahanas*, the phrase *adhi rocane* is [to be supplied] just as in *agniṃ yunajmi*. In *antarikṣaṃ sūryaḥ* and *sūryo 'ntarikṣam*, [the word *antarikṣam* is supplied after *sūryaḥ*]. In *iṣe tvā upavīḥ*, the phrase *bhavataṃ naḥ samanasaḥ* is [to be supplied] just as in *samitam*. In *adya no naḥ adya adya naḥ*, [the repetition is for emphasis]. In *nigrāhyāḥ*, the phrase *drapsaśca skanda* is [to be supplied] just as in *abhyasthāt*. And in the section beginning with *dhruvāsī*, [the word *asi* is supplied after each *anu yaḥ*].

In the passage "anu yo yo'nvanu yaḥ santvāsiñcāmi," the phrase "sahasvārātīḥ" is [to be repeated] just as in the case of "dhruvā sī. Thus: "sahasvārātīyataḥ, arātīyataḥ sahasva, sahasvārātīyataḥ. (72)

He states the rule regarding *jaṭā*, *malopa*, and so forth: in the *yājyā* "tvamagne rudra," the phrase "agne pavasva svapā" [is treated] just as in "aganma suvar. In "asme varco varco asme asme varcaḥ," the phrase "tvamagne vratapā" [is treated] just as in "daivīṃ dhiyam. In "tvamagne agne tvaṃ tvamagne," because it is both mantra and brāhmaṇa, it remains exactly as it is, just as in "vāg vai devebhyaḥ. For example:

Other examples have been stated. In the case of *dhruvāsī*, the phrase *yāste agne* applies here, just as in the case of *vayo vā agniḥ*. Thus: *te agne*, *agne te*, *te te agne*. Why [is the rule] stated as *sūrye pare*? Because in the passage *yāste agne samidho yāni*, there is simply elision (*lopa*) at the time of forming the *jaṭā* recitation. For example: *te agne*, *gne te*, *te te agne*. In the passage *imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām*, the phrase *dyauṣṭe pṛṣṭham* applies in exactly the same way even within the thirty-question section (*traiṃśika-praśna*).

The three questions beginning with "That which is called the *traiṃśika* is that by which one... are as follows: regarding the question "Or he who [acts] contrary to the deity," it is as in the passage: "The ocean is the intermediate space; the intermediate space is the ocean; in the intermediate space is the ocean. Regarding the mantra "Thou art the caul of the ruling power (*kṣatra*)," the sentence is "May life be perfected through sacrifice. Regarding the mantra "And the embryos," it is as follows: "May the out-breath be perfected; may the out-breath be perfected; may the out-breath be perfected."

In the *yājyā* "tvamagnerudra," the phrase "āyurdā agne" occurs as it does in the third section of the third book (*tṛtīyakāṇḍe tṛtīyapraśne*). In that *anuvāka*, it says: "āyurdā agne, agne āyurdā, āyurdā agne. In the same way, it also occurs here in the passage "āyurdā agne haviṣo juṣāṇa" regarding the *avabhṛtha*, because it belongs to the Brāhmaṇa portion. In the passage "kṣatrasyolbamasi," the phrase "vājaśca prasavaśca" occurs, just as in the passage "ekācama. Furthermore, it says: "cāpija āpijaśca cāpijaḥ."

In the section beginning with *dhruvakṣitiḥ*, the phrase *apānaṃ me* occurs in both of the two sections starting with *indrāgnī avyathamānām* and *bhūyaskṛdasi*. For example: *apānaṃ me apānamapānaṃ me*. In the section beginning with *agniṃ yunajmi*, the phrase *yenā sahasram* occurs in the section beginning with *yadākūtāt*. For example: *yenāgne agne yena yenāgne*. In the section beginning with *yenāsahasram*, the phrase *paro'gne* likewise occurs again.

In the *ṛc*s and Brāhmaṇa passages, by the statement "sufficient with two or three words, etc.," both of the following two sentences—"parognah" (which is joined with "dakṣiṇā") and "yenāgne sukṛtaḥ pathā"—are said to be without elision (*alopa*). [The forms are: *yena agne* (repeated as *yena yena agne*), *agne sukṛtaḥ* (repeated as *sukṛtaḥ agne agne sukṛtaḥ*), and *agne dakṣiṇāḥ* (repeated as *dakṣiṇā agne agne dakṣiṇāḥ*). Because they are joined with other elements here, the rule regarding the three-word sequence (*tripada-nyāya*) does not apply.

In the mantra *agniṃ yunajmi*, the phrase *asminthsadhasthe* occurs; just as in *yadākūtāt*. [The repetition is] *asmin thsadhasthe sadhasthe asminnasmin thsadhasthe*. In the mantra *imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām*, the phrase *āgatyavājī* occurs; just as in *vyṛddhaṃ vā*. [The repetition is] *vājyaddhvano addhvano vājī vājyaddhvanaḥ*. This is called "non-identity" (*anaikya*) because there is no unity [of form]. The meaning is that there is no elision (*alopa*). 74.

He states the rule beginning with "tripada" (three-word sequence) regarding the *jaṭā* (intertwined recitation): "Having stepped from path to path," "having stepped from path to path," "he exists before, before he exists," "the purifier bestows, the purifier bestows, the purifier bestows. The meaning is that this applies to subjects consisting of three words or more. "O Aṅgiras, thus," "O Aṅgiras, thus"—this is the [example]. 75.

In the case of *agne aṅgiraḥ*, since there is no occurrence of three or more words [beginning with that term], the application [of the rule] occurs because of the explicit mention of *aṅgiro phsuya*. Thus, *aṅgira itītyaṅgiro aṅgiraḥ*. In the case of *tantvā samidbhiraṅgiraḥ*, it is likewise *aṅgira itītyaṅgiro aṅgiraḥ*. The sentence *ukhyetā asya sūdadohasaḥ* is treated in exactly the same way even in the *traiṃśika* [section]: *asya sūdadohasassūdado haso asyāsya sūdado hasaḥ*.

"‘Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre’—thus I dedicate this forest to that [deity]; ‘vidhema te parama’—" in this manner, wherever it is to be seen according to the various divisions of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, it should be understood exactly so. 76. Jaṭāmaṇitā aparyantaṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ śrīmate Hayagrīvāya namaḥ.
